title: PM: India to add 500 GW non-fossil fuel capacity in the next 10-11 years
syllabus: GS3 › Infrastructure: energy; Climate change; Investment models · GS2 › International agreements (Paris Agreement)
summary: At the Bharat Renewable Energy Summit, the PM set a goal of adding 500 GW of non-fossil capacity in 10–11 years, noting India met its Paris target of half its capacity from non-fossil sources five years early.
evolution: Editorial: E100 alone will not secure energy; diesel dominates oil demand.
Editorial page: energy security depends on electrification and how we do it.
PM sets a 500 GW non-fossil capacity addition goal for the next decade.
ideas: Early delivery on Paris: India pledged that half its installed power capacity would be non-fossil and met it in 2025, five years ahead of schedule.
GS2 · Paris Agreement / GS3 · Climate
Meeting the Paris non-fossil capacity target five years early strengthens India's credibility in climate negotiations.
A bigger next step: the PM announced 500 GW of new non-fossil capacity over the next 10–11 years, calling the target difficult but achievable.
GS3 · Energy transition
India's new 500 GW goal signals that the energy transition is moving from targets met to scale-up.
Clean energy as energy security: the PM said clean-energy investment helped India avert a worse energy crisis during the West Asia war.
GS3 · Energy security / GS2 · Foreign policy
Domestic clean power insulates India from fossil-fuel shocks abroad.
Investment drives the shift: the PM cited large flows into renewables over the past decade and big opportunities ahead.
GS3 · Investment
Sustained private investment is what turns renewable targets into installed capacity.
Capacity is not yet generation: a majority of installed capacity is non-fossil, but intermittent sources need storage, grids and flexible supply to deliver reliable power.
GS3 · Infrastructure
Installed capacity must be matched by storage and transmission to become reliable clean electricity.

answer.t: Having met its Paris target early, India's next test is turning capacity into reliable, round-the-clock clean power.

title: Steel policy for 2047 needs to shift focus — from protection to competition
where: The Ideas Page, page 9 (Montek S Ahluwalia, Shishir Gupta & Rishita Sachdeva, CSEP)
syllabus: GS3 › Industrial policy and its effect on growth; Effects of liberalisation; Mineral resources · GS1 › Distribution of industries and mineral resources; Effects of globalisation · GS2 › Government policies
summary: On the Draft National Steel Policy: Vision 2047, the writers argue Indian steel is profitable because it is protected, not efficient, and that duties, quality-control orders and the iron-ore export duty must be phased down.
ideas: Big but not yet competitive: India has risen to the world's second-largest steel producer, but the draft policy's goal of global competitiveness needs a clear meaning, as high profits come from protection, not efficiency.
GS3 · Industrial policy
High profitability under protection is not the same as global competitiveness.
Cheap ore, underpaid states: a 30% export duty on high-grade iron ore keeps domestic ore far below global prices, subsidising steelmakers at the cost of mineral-rich regions and exploration.
GS3 · Mineral policy / GS1 · Resource regions
Export duties on ore transfer value from mineral-rich regions to steelmakers and discourage mining.
Protection hurts users of steel: import duties and Quality Control Orders make Indian steel costlier than even high-cost Japan, raising costs for construction, automobiles and export-oriented MSMEs.
GS3 · Industry / MSMEs
Protecting an input industry taxes every industry that uses it, especially MSME exporters.

Competition did not kill other industries: tariff cuts in pharmaceuticals and auto components were followed by rising shares in global exports; steel should cut duties to ASEAN levels over five years and drop QCOs.
GS3 · Liberalisation / Trade
Pharma and auto parts show that lower protection can raise, not reduce, export competitiveness.

Reform the structure, not just tariffs: consider privatising some public-sector plants, remove the ore export duty and overhaul mining policy that discourages exploration (explorers must surrender discovered mines to auction).
GS3 · PSU reform / Mining
Competitive steel needs privatisation of laggard PSUs and a mining policy that rewards exploration.
